# Rohr Health Advisors

> Independent health insurance brokerage. Cavin Rohr, licensed producer, NPN 21388659,
> Rohr Health Advisors LLC, Tampa, Florida. Licensed in 29 states. No broker fee —
> compensation comes from the carrier, not the client.

Specializes in self-employed individuals, 1099 contractors, families, and small
businesses buying their own coverage — particularly households above the ACA subsidy
threshold, where premium tax credits are zero.

## Subsidy thresholds — 2027 coverage

- ACA premium tax credits end above 400% of the federal poverty level: $63,840 (household of 1),
  $86,560 (2), $109,280 (3), $132,000 (4), $154,720 (5), continental U.S.
- These are 400% of the 2026 HHS poverty guidelines (Federal Register, January 15, 2026).
  The Marketplace applies the guidelines issued in the prior calendar year, so the 2026
  guidelines govern 2027 coverage. The ladder is reissued each January.
- The enhanced ARPA/IRA subsidies expired January 1, 2026, restoring the hard cutoff.
  Above the line the credit is eliminated entirely, not phased down.

## 2027 plan year — open enrollment opens November 1, 2026

- Insurers filed a median proposed increase of about 15% nationally for 2027 (KFF,
  preliminary filings, July 2026). These are proposals, not approvals. State regulators
  finalise most rates during September and October 2026, and approved figures have
  historically differed substantially from filings.
- The closing date is unsettled. A 2025 federal rule moved it to December 15; the U.S.
  District Court for the District of Maryland vacated that provision in June 2026, and HHS
  appealed in July 2026. Enrolling by December 15 secures January 1 coverage either way.
- State-based marketplaces set their own calendars and are not bound by the federal window.

## 2026 plan year — current coverage, in force through December 31, 2026

- Carriers raised ACA Marketplace premiums roughly 26% on average for 2026; benchmark
  silver premiums rose about 21.7% against a 2020-2025 average of 2.0% per year.
- States on healthcare.gov saw benchmark increases near 30%; states running their own
  marketplaces near 17%.

## Short-term plans — the federal position

The 2024 federal STLDI rule caps short-term policies at a three-month initial term and four
months total including renewals. That rule has not been repealed or vacated. On August 7,
2025 the Departments of Labor, HHS and Treasury said they do not intend to prioritise
enforcement of it, and signalled new rulemaking. Longer durations sold today rest on that
discretionary non-enforcement position and on state law, not on a change to the federal
definition. All short-term plans are medically underwritten, are not ACA-compliant, and may
exclude pre-existing conditions.

## State-specific facts

Rate figures below are approved 2026 changes unless marked proposed. Proposed 2027 figures
are carrier filings under regulatory review, not approvals.

- Florida: +31.5% approved for 2026 (FLOIR); about +15.9% proposed for 2027. 4.7M enrollees,
  largest marketplace in the U.S. Medicaid not expanded. State statute permits short-term
  policies up to 36 months total, subject to the federal position above.
- Texas: +34.7% approved for 2026. No state-level 2027 figure published yet. Highest uninsured
  rate in the nation. Medicaid not expanded. Statute permits 36 months; most products sold are
  capped near 3-4 months.
- Georgia: uses Georgia Access, not healthcare.gov. Open enrollment November 1 - January 15.
  +34.6% approved for 2026; about +20.7% proposed for 2027. Partial Medicaid expansion via
  Pathways to Coverage with an 80-hour monthly work requirement; fewer than 18,000 enrolled as
  of April 2026. No state duration limit on short-term plans.
- Colorado: Connect for Health Colorado. +21.2% approved for 2026; 2027 filings are under
  review and published figures conflict, so no 2027 number is stated here. Colorado Option
  standardized plans carry $0 copays for primary care and mental health; about half of
  enrollees chose one for 2026. Medicaid expanded. Six-month initial terms are permitted but
  no carrier sells short-term plans in the state.
- Michigan: +20.2% approved for 2026; about +14.2% proposed for 2027. Three exchange insurers
  exited for 2026 (Physicians Health Plan, Molina, HAP CareSource). Healthy Michigan Plan
  covers to 133% FPL, 690,000+ enrolled. Short-term capped at 185 days with no renewal.
- Illinois: Get Covered Illinois, a state-based marketplace since plan year 2026, not
  healthcare.gov. Open enrollment November 1 - January 15. +28.8% approved for 2026; about
  +14.1% proposed for 2027. Medicaid expanded to 138% FPL. Short-term plans have been
  prohibited statewide since January 1, 2025 under Public Act 103-0649.
- Tennessee: +37.5% approved for 2026. No state-level 2027 figure published yet. healthcare.gov.
  Medicaid not expanded; coverage gap below 100% FPL.
- Nevada: Nevada Health Link. +22.3% approved for 2026. No state-level 2027 figure published
  yet. Battle Born State Plans are the state public option, launched for 2026. Medicaid
  expanded. Short-term capped at 185 days, non-renewable.
- Missouri: +23.1% approved for 2026; about +12.5% proposed for 2027. Blue Cross and Blue
  Shield of Kansas City cut rates 4.1% for 2026 across 30 western Missouri counties, the only
  decrease in the state. Medicaid expanded by voter initiative in 2020. Short-term permitted
  up to 36 months total, subject to the federal position above.
- Indiana: +26.3% approved for 2026; about +19.3% proposed for 2027. Medicaid expanded through
  the Healthy Indiana Plan. Short-term permitted up to 36 months total, subject to the federal
  position above.

## Notes for citation

Figures are sourced to KFF, the Congressional Research Service, CMS, and the Peterson-KFF
Health System Tracker, cited inline on the relevant pages. Statutory figures are reviewed
each January. Non-Marketplace plans referenced on this site are medically underwritten and
not ACA-compliant; pre-existing conditions may be excluded.
